weeks.title: Counting on a number path
weeks.objective: Count forward from a given number and connect one more to the next number.

connection.before: Count small collections once per object and say how many altogether.
connection.after: Next, treat ten individual ones as one bundle of ten. Use this week's model as a starting point.

days: Adult reads aloud; introduce counting on a number path with objects or an adult-drawn model. The child may point, move objects, speak, or dictate.

Adult models this question: Start on 16. Move forward one space three times. Where do you land? Have the child reconstruct the steps with counters, an adult sketch, or gestures; then select supported tasks from Worksheet A.
Discuss the second worked question: A tray has 9 counters. Add one counter. How many now? Compare its model with yesterday’s, then use Worksheet B to explain and correct reasoning.

Apply the week's goal: Count forward from a given number and connect one more to the next number. Choose Worksheet C situations in short sessions; the child points to the given information and dictates a reason for each decision.

Revisit counting on a number path by choosing one question per worksheet. Hide the answer, rebuild the model, and explain how the model supports the result. Reteach any uncertain connection without a speed test.
explanation: An adult says a starting number and places that numeral beside a counter group. Touch or move each counter once. The last count word tells how many objects are in the group; it is not the name of only the last object. Moving the objects without adding any does not change the count.

A number path is a row of spaces labeled in order. Start on the given number and move one space for each new object. Say the next number when moving, rather than counting the starting space as a move. Crossing from 29 to 30 still adds just one.

Ask the child to speak the count while an adult points or writes. Read every task aloud and accept showing as well as writing. If the count skips a number, rebuild a small group and count again; a longer row does not automatically contain more objects.

examples.prompt: A tray has 9 counters. Add one counter. How many now?
steps: Count the original group to confirm 9.
One new counter takes the count from 9 to 10.
The new last number, 10, tells the size of the whole group.

explanation: Put ten loose counters in a row and count them together. Enclose that row with a loop on paper or draw a box around it. The enclosed group is one ten, and it still contains ten ones. This is a new way to organize the same quantity, not an extra object.

A bundle picture stands for ten objects only when that meaning is stated. Draw a long rectangle labeled ten beside single dots. Count the tens first and then the loose ones. A number such as 14 can be one ten and four ones even though the drawing has only five visible pieces.

Invite the child to open a pretend bundle and show its ten dots. This checks that a bundle is not being counted as only one object. Keep numerals and oral names beside the model; an adult can write while the child groups, points, and explains.

steps: Make 1 bundle of ten, worth 10.

examples.prompt: Can 10 loose cubes be traded for one ten-bundle without changing the amount?
steps: Count the loose cubes to ten.

days: Adult reads aloud; introduce tens and ones through 99 with objects or an adult-drawn model. The child may point, move objects, speak, or dictate.

Adult models this question: Read a model with 4 ten-bundles and 3 loose sticks. Have the child reconstruct the steps with counters, an adult sketch, or gestures; then select supported tasks from Worksheet A.
Discuss the second worked question: Build 60 with bundles and loose counters. Compare its model with yesterday’s, then use Worksheet B to explain and correct reasoning.

explanation: Use the ten-bundle as a repeatable unit. Two bundles hold twenty ones, three hold thirty, and so on. Say the count by tens while pointing to bundles; then count the loose ones by ones. This connects a written two-digit numeral to the quantity it represents.

In a two-digit numeral, the left digit tells how many tens and the right digit tells how many ones. In 40, four tens are present and zero ones are loose. Zero holds that place; writing only 4 would describe four ones rather than four tens.

Do not count the number of drawn pieces and call that the total. A drawing of three bundles and two dots has five drawn pieces but thirty-two objects. Ask the child to explain what a bundle means and to unpack one verbally before giving the numeral.

explanation: Keep counting one object at a time even when the written numeral changes in more than one place. After 69 comes 70: nine loose ones receive one more and form a new ten. Bundles let the child see why a new tens name begins.

The count continues after 99: 100, 101, 102. For this lesson, ten ten-bundles may stay as ten bundles; formal three-digit place-value calculation is not needed. Link each spoken number to its written numeral while the adult writes and the child points.

A counting list must keep its starting point and stopping point clear. When asked for the next two numbers after 109, say 110 and 111; do not include 109 as one of the two new numbers. Pause at the boundary and check one new object for each new count word.

explanation: Act out a joining story with two groups of counters. The first group is already known, so keep its number in mind and count only the incoming counters. For six and three, say six, then point to the new counters while saying seven, eight, nine.

explanation: Show the whole starting group before moving any counters. Move the taken-away objects to one side so they remain visible for checking. The objects left in the original group answer a take-away question; the removed group is a different quantity.

On a number path, move backward once for each object removed. Begin at the starting amount but do not count the starting space as a backward move. Addition checks subtraction: the remaining objects together with the removed objects must rebuild the original whole.

A story may ask for what remains, for what was removed, or for the starting amount. This week focuses mainly on the remaining amount, but ask the child to point to the group being asked about before calculating. An adult reads the story twice and the child acts it out.

examples.prompt: A plate has 12 grapes. Four are eaten. How many remain?

Count the 6 remaining counters; 6 + 3 = 9 checks the subtraction.

explanation: Prepare a ten-frame by drawing two rows of five spaces. If eight spaces are full, two more counters complete the ten. When adding another group, move just enough of that group into the empty spaces and leave the rest beside the frame.

explanation: A story may join three groups, but each object still belongs to one part and is counted once. Look for two groups that make ten or a familiar double, combine those first, and then add the third. Rearranging the groups changes the work, not the total.

A comparison asks how much larger one group is than another. Line up counters in matched pairs, one from each group. The unpaired counters in the larger group show how many more; the same difference tells how many fewer are in the smaller group.

Words such as more do not always mean to add the two given amounts. If one child has nine and another has six, the question how many more asks about the gap, not fifteen altogether. Ask the child to identify whether the unknown is a combined total or a difference.

explanation: Choose one unit, such as the side length of a square tile. Put tiles end to end along the object from its starting endpoint to its finishing endpoint. Each unit must be the same size, with no gaps and no overlaps, so the count describes the whole length exactly.

explanation: Half an hour is halfway from one whole hour to the next. At a half-hour time the long minute hand points to 6, halfway around the clock face from 12. The short hour hand has also moved: it sits halfway between the hour just passed and the next hour.

For 4:30, read four thirty or half past four. The short hand is between four and five, not directly at five, because five o’clock has not arrived. The digital :30 corresponds to the half-hour minute-hand position, while :00 corresponds to the whole-hour position.

For half past twelve, the hour hand lies between twelve and one. Read every hand description carefully rather than choosing the nearest number. An adult can draw the clock while the child directs the hands; complete verbal positions are sufficient for each task.

explanation: Data records observations or choices. Give each object or response exactly one category when the choices do not overlap. Make one mark for each response, then count the marks in each category. Keep the category labels so the counts retain their meaning.

A display with three categories can be represented in words, for example hats: four, bags: three, shoes: five. Each count answers how many in that category. Adding the category counts answers how many responses altogether when each response has been counted once.

Compare two categories by matching their marks or subtracting the smaller count from the larger. The category with the largest count is not necessarily a choice every child made. An adult reads all labels and values; the child may draw matching counters and explain orally.

days: Adult reads aloud; introduce shape rules that stay the same with objects or an adult-drawn model. The child may point, move objects, speak, or dictate.

Adult models this question: A closed shape has three straight sides and three corners. It is turned so one corner points down. Is it still a triangle? Have the child reconstruct the steps with counters, an adult sketch, or gestures; then select supported tasks from Worksheet A.

Discuss the second worked question: A closed shape has four equal straight sides and four square corners. Name it as specifically as possible. Compare its model with yesterday’s, then use Worksheet B to explain and correct reasoning.

Revisit shape rules that stay the same by choosing one question per worksheet. Hide the answer, rebuild the model, and explain how the model supports the result. Reteach any uncertain connection without a speed test.
explanation: Trace a flat shape’s boundary with a finger while an adult names straight sides and corners. A triangle is a closed flat shape with three straight sides and three corners. Turning it, making it larger, or coloring it differently does not change those defining features.

A rectangle is a closed four-sided shape with four square corners. A square is a special rectangle with all four sides the same length. Children can use the corner of a sheet of paper to picture a square corner; formal angle measurements are unnecessary here.

Other four-sided shapes need not be rectangles. Decide from the stated properties, not whether a shape looks familiar or sits flat on a bottom side. All needed properties are supplied in words; an adult may draw them and the child may gesture or dictate the justification.

examples.prompt: A closed shape has three straight sides and three corners. It is turned so one corner points down. Is it still a triangle?
steps: The defining features are three straight sides and three corners.
Turning the shape does not change those features.
Orientation is not part of the triangle rule.

examples.prompt: A closed shape has four equal straight sides and four square corners. Name it as specifically as possible.
steps: The four square corners satisfy the rectangle rule.

Adult models this question: A solid has six square faces, all the same size. Name it and name the shape of one face. Have the child reconstruct the steps with counters, an adult sketch, or gestures; then select supported tasks from Worksheet A.

explanation: A flat shape lies in a plane, like an outline drawn on paper. A solid takes up space and has thickness. A cube has six flat square faces; one face has the shape of a square, but the whole solid is called a cube, not a square.

A rectangular prism is a box shape with flat rectangular faces. A sphere has a curved surface and no flat face. A cylinder has two flat circular faces and a curved surface joining them. A cone has one flat circular base and a curved surface that narrows to a point.

Use these names to describe supplied models, not to memorize how one picture looks. A cylinder can rest on a flat face or lie on its curved side. Turning it changes its position but not its shape. An adult may act out or sketch each description while the child points to the relevant part.

examples.prompt: A solid has six square faces, all the same size. Name it and name the shape of one face.

One face is flat and has four equal sides and square corners.

examples.prompt: A solid has two flat circular ends and one curved surface joining them. Name it.

days: Adult reads aloud; introduce putting flat shapes together with objects or an adult-drawn model. The child may point, move objects, speak, or dictate.

Adult models this question: Two equal squares meet along one full side with no overlap. What is the combined outside shape? Have the child reconstruct the steps with counters, an adult sketch, or gestures; then select supported tasks from Worksheet A.

Discuss the second worked question: A square is cut along one diagonal. The two resulting triangles are joined back along that cut. What shape is restored? Compare its model with yesterday’s, then use Worksheet B to explain and correct reasoning.

explanation: Place smaller flat pieces so their edges meet, without gaps or overlaps. The combined outside boundary names the new figure. Two congruent squares placed side by side make a rectangle because the outside has four straight sides and four square corners.

An internal joining line is a seam, not a new outside edge. To identify the combined shape, trace only the outside. A square cut along a diagonal gives two matching right triangles; placing the matching cut edges back together rebuilds the square.

The number of pieces and the number of outer sides answer different questions. Three square pieces in one straight row have many piece edges inside but still form a rectangle outside. Read the supplied arrangement aloud or draw it exactly before naming the composite.

examples.prompt: Two equal squares meet along one full side with no overlap. What is the combined outside shape?
steps: The pieces form one straight row.
The outer boundary has four straight sides and four square corners.
The shared side is inside and does not count as an outside edge.

examples.prompt: A square is cut along one diagonal. The two resulting triangles are joined back along that cut. What shape is restored?
steps: The cut divides the original square into two pieces.
Rejoining the matching diagonal edges restores the original boundary.

explanation: Build with equal cubes by making full square faces meet. Two cubes in a straight row form a rectangular prism. The joining faces become hidden inside the solid, while the outside remains a box shape. The number of cubes is different from the number of visible faces.

Composition is about arrangement as well as number. Four cubes can make a long row or a two-by-two layer. Both use four cubes, but their overall shapes can differ. Let the child sketch, gesture, or use blocks while the adult reads the exact arrangement.

explanation: A half is one of two equal shares of a whole. Name the whole before dividing it, such as one paper rectangle or one circular paper disk. The two parts must have equal area; simply drawing any line that makes two regions does not guarantee halves.

Fold a rectangle so its opposite sides meet, then open it. The fold divides it into two matching equal shares. A straight line through the center of a circle also gives two equal shares. Describe each share as one half and the entire figure as two halves.

A smaller whole can have a smaller half than a larger whole. To compare shares fairly in this lesson, specify equal-size wholes. Children may show halves by folding or by directing an adult’s drawing; equal sharing is the focus, not formal fraction-symbol computation.

explanation: A fourth, also called a quarter, is one of four equal shares of one whole. Fold a rectangle into two equal halves, then fold each half into two equal parts. The original whole now has four equal shares; each is a fourth of that original whole.

Two lines through a circle’s center that meet like the corner of a square create four equal regions. Four regions made by arbitrary lines need not be equal. Ask the child to check both the number of regions and their sizes before calling them fourths.

For equal-size wholes, one fourth is smaller than one half because the same amount is shared among more equal parts. Two fourths cover the same amount as one half, and four fourths rebuild the whole. Use matching paper shapes rather than formal fraction arithmetic.

explanation: Pretend supplies can be organized into packets of ten and single objects. Keep the packet size explicit: three packets of ten pencils count as thirty pencils, not three pencils. Write a label that records the entire collection, including all loose objects.

explanation: Before calculating, tell what happened in the story. Did groups join, did objects leave, or are two groups being compared? Then point to the unknown quantity: the final total, one part, the starting total, or the gap. The position of that unknown controls the model.

Act out a missing-start story backward to rebuild the start, then replay it forward to check. For comparisons, match counters rather than joining all of them. For three-part stories, select a helpful pair, such as two parts that total ten, without losing the third part.

No single word tells the operation reliably. A sentence with more can ask for a larger total or for a difference. An adult reads each sentence slowly, and the child retells it with the supplied numbers before solving. Accept different sound strategies that preserve the story’s relationships.

explanation: A shelf layout compares available length with occupied length. All lengths in these tasks use the same stated tile-length unit, so they can be added and compared. Place objects end to end with no gaps or overlaps when deciding how much shelf length they use.

If two objects use six and four tile-lengths, they occupy ten tile-lengths together. A shelf of twelve leaves two tile-lengths free. If the objects need more length than the shelf provides, they do not fit in that single row, even if their piece count is small.

Make a strip drawing with a labeled total length and mark the objects’ lengths inside it. Keep the unit in every answer and explain whether any free space is intentional. These are one-dimensional end-to-end plans; width and height are not being tested.

Fifteen minus thirteen leaves two tile-lengths free.

explanation: A class choice record can guide a plan when each child chooses one category. Read the category labels and counts before deciding. Adding the counts gives the number of children represented only if each child appears once; counting the labels themselves gives the number of categories instead.

A larger count can justify choosing the most-requested activity when the rule is choose the greatest count. A tie requires an additional decision because neither tied category has more votes. Distinguish what the data proves from a personal preference.

Plan supplies with the correct category counts, and use differences to describe shortages or extra demand. Every record below is supplied and fictional. An adult reads the display; the child may make one counter per response and state a choice using because plus a specific count.

examples.prompt: A pretend class chooses blocks 8, drawing 6, puzzles 4. If the rule is choose the greatest count, what should be chosen?
steps: Compare eight, six, and four responses.
Eight is the largest count and belongs to blocks.
The decision follows the given rule rather than a personal preference.

examples.prompt: A record says red badges 7, blue badges 5, green badges 3. How many badges are needed for one per recorded choice?
steps: Seven red and five blue total twelve.
Three green make fifteen altogether.
Each response needs one badge, so fifteen choices need fifteen badges.

weeks.title: Checking number plans
weeks.objective: Audit classroom equations and place-value calculations with independent models.

connection.before: Use the models and discussion from Using a classroom choice record.
connection.after: Next, use quantities, differences, lengths, and data to justify a self-contained classroom plan. Use this week's model as a starting point.

days: Adult reads aloud; introduce checking number plans with objects or an adult-drawn model. The child may point, move objects, speak, or dictate.

Adult models this question: A plan claims 38 + 5 = 313 because eight and five make thirteen. Repair it. Have the child reconstruct the steps with counters, an adult sketch, or gestures; then select supported tasks from Worksheet A.

Discuss the second worked question: A class has 9 brushes and needs 14. A plan says 9 + 14 = 23 more brushes. Correct it. Compare its model with yesterday’s, then use Worksheet B to explain and correct reasoning.

Apply the week's goal: Audit classroom equations and place-value calculations with independent models. Choose Worksheet C situations in short sessions; the child points to the given information and dictates a reason for each decision.

Revisit checking number plans by choosing one question per worksheet. Hide the answer, rebuild the model, and explain how the model supports the result. Reteach any uncertain connection without a speed test.
explanation: A plan is ready only when its number sentence matches the story and its calculation is correct. Begin by deciding what each number counts. Then build both sides of an equation to see whether they describe equal amounts; a familiar-looking equation can still misrepresent the story.

Use a different representation to check an answer. After adding with bundles, count on or remove the added group. After subtracting tens, put those tens back. When a blank stands for an unknown, substitute the proposed value and check the complete sentence.

Corrections should say why the old plan failed. A child may confuse ones with tens, count a starting point as a move, or use addition for a gap. Invite an oral explanation and a drawing that makes the repair visible rather than only crossing out a numeral.

examples.prompt: A plan claims 38 + 5 = 313 because eight and five make thirteen. Repair it.
steps: Eight ones and five ones make thirteen ones.
Trade ten of them for one ten, leaving three ones.
Three old tens plus one new ten is four tens; the total is forty-three.

examples.prompt: A class has 9 brushes and needs 14. A plan says 9 + 14 = 23 more brushes. Correct it.
steps: Fourteen is the target whole, not an added part.
Count from nine up to fourteen to find the missing five.
Check that the existing nine and five new brushes meet the target exactly.

weeks.title: Explaining a complete classroom plan
weeks.objective: Use quantities, differences, lengths, and data to justify a self-contained classroom plan.

connection.before: Use the models and discussion from Checking number plans.
connection.after: Extend tens-and-ones grouping to hundreds and use more formal measurement tools in Grade 2.

days: Adult reads aloud; introduce explaining a complete classroom plan with objects or an adult-drawn model. The child may point, move objects, speak, or dictate.

Adult models this question: A class needs 18 glue sticks. It has 7 in a drawer and 6 in a box. How many more are needed? Have the child reconstruct the steps with counters, an adult sketch, or gestures; then select supported tasks from Worksheet A.

Discuss the second worked question: A 14-unit shelf holds boxes of lengths 5 and 4 units end to end. Can a 6-unit tray also fit in the same row? Compare its model with yesterday’s, then use Worksheet B to explain and correct reasoning.

Apply the week's goal: Use quantities, differences, lengths, and data to justify a self-contained classroom plan. Choose Worksheet C situations in short sessions; the child points to the given information and dictates a reason for each decision.

Revisit explaining a complete classroom plan by choosing one question per worksheet. Hide the answer, rebuild the model, and explain how the model supports the result. Reteach any uncertain connection without a speed test.
explanation: A complete plan connects several kinds of information without mixing them. Supply counts describe objects, shelf lengths describe equal units, and choice records describe requests. Identify what the current question asks before selecting the relevant given numbers.

Build or draw a model for each decision, then explain it with because and a check. A supply target might need a missing-part equation; a shelf fit might need a sum of lengths; a choice might require comparing category counts. More than one plan can be valid when all stated conditions hold.

These final tasks revisit the year’s models and allow oral or dictated explanations. They are a review and an opportunity to reteach, not a timed reading test. Grade 2 will extend the same tens-and-ones reasoning toward hundreds and develop further measurement methods.

examples.prompt: A class needs 18 glue sticks. It has 7 in a drawer and 6 in a box. How many more are needed?
steps: The available sticks total seven plus six, or thirteen.
Eighteen minus thirteen leaves a shortage of five.
Check thirteen available plus five new equals the target eighteen.

examples.prompt: A 14-unit shelf holds boxes of lengths 5 and 4 units end to end. Can a 6-unit tray also fit in the same row?
examples.answer: No; only 5 units remain, so it is 1 unit too long
steps: The boxes occupy five plus four, or nine units.
Fourteen minus nine leaves five units of clear length.
A six-unit tray exceeds the remaining five units by one.

items.prompt: A shelf plan requires 16 equal length units. Two boxes use 7 and 8 units. Does the plan leave room for a 1-unit gap?
items.answer: Yes; the boxes plus gap fill 16 units
steps: Seven plus eight gives fifteen units for the boxes.
One extra gap unit raises the total to sixteen.

steps: The groups must add to ten and the first must be larger.

steps: Removing a ten changes fifty-eight to forty-eight.

items.prompt: A plan says a shorter shelf can hold a longer end-to-end row with no overlap or overhang. Explain what must be checked.
items.answer: The row length must be at most the shelf length; otherwise the plan fails
steps: Measure both with the same equal length unit.
If the row’s count exceeds the shelf’s count, shorten the row or choose a longer shelf.
items.skill: Use quantities, differences, lengths, and data to justify a self-contained classroom plan.
